With the right outlet, they are a joy: affectionate, playful, and up for any adventure. Without one, they become restless and anxious, and may herd kids, chase cars, or chew. Their herding instinct can include nipping at heels.

Australian Shepherds thrive when their days include real exercise and something to think about, such as herding, agility, frisbee, obedience, or advanced trick training. They are a great match for active owners and a frustrating one for people who want a calm house dog.
livingWith:
Expect a dog that wants to be with you and doing something, every day. Aussies need lots of exercise and mental work, and are happiest with a yard and an owner who hikes, runs, or trains. They shed heavily, especially twice a year. Many are sensitive to sound and movement and can be reactive to fast-moving things like bikes or kids running if not trained.

They can be wonderful with children when raised with them and taught not to herd. Early socialization helps balance their natural reserve with strangers. They do not do well left alone for long workdays.
healthCareGuide:
Ask breeders for OFA hip and elbow results, an eye exam, and DNA tests for MDR1, hereditary cataracts (HSF4), and progressive retinal atrophy. The MDR1 mutation makes dogs sensitive to certain common drugs, including some antiparasitic and anti-diarrhea medications, so tell your vet your dog's MDR1 status.

Epilepsy occurs in the breed. Avoid puppies from merle-to-merle breedings: 'double merles' have a high risk of deafness and blindness. Aussies are otherwise a fairly robust breed when bred carefully.
funFact: Despite the name, Australian Shepherds were actually developed in the American West.
famousQuote: A brilliant, high-drive herding dog from the American West that needs a job and an owner who loves to stay busy.
funFacts: Despite the name, the Australian Shepherd was developed in the United States.
Many Aussies have eyes of two different colors, and some have eyes split between two colors.
Jay Sisler's trick-performing Aussies became rodeo celebrities in the 1950s and 1960s.
Aussies are commonly born with naturally short tails; the breed has a gene for natural bobtails.
commonMisconceptions: That they come from Australia; the breed was developed in the American West. Another misconception is that a backyard is enough exercise. Aussies need active time with their people, and mental challenges, to be calm at home.
idealOwnerProfile: Very active people and families who love training, outdoor activities, or dog sports, and want a smart, devoted partner. Great for rural homes and anyone who wants a dog to do things with.
notGoodFor: Apartment living without lots of outdoor time, owners who work long hours away from home, people who want a low-energy companion, and homes not prepared for heavy shedding.
groomingGuide: Brush two to three times a week with a slicker brush and undercoat rake, paying attention to the feathering behind the ears, the pants, and the tail. Brush daily during seasonal sheds. Do not shave the double coat. Trim nails, check ears, and brush teeth regularly.

faqs.question: How much exercise does an Australian Shepherd need?
faqs.answer: A lot: plan on 90 minutes or more of activity a day, mixing physical exercise with training or herding-style games. Without it, Aussies often become anxious or destructive.

faqs.question: Are Australian Shepherds good family dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, for active families. They are loyal and affectionate but may try to herd children and need lots of activity and structure.

faqs.question: Do Australian Shepherds shed a lot?
faqs.answer: Yes. Their medium-length double coat sheds year-round and heavily in spring and fall. Regular brushing helps.

faqs.question: What is the MDR1 gene in Australian Shepherds?
faqs.answer: A gene mutation that makes some dogs sensitive to certain common medications. A simple DNA test tells you your dog's status so your vet can choose safe drugs.

faqs.question: Are Australian Shepherds good for first-time owners?
faqs.answer: They can be for very active first-timers who are committed to training, but their intelligence and energy make them demanding. Many first-time owners find them a lot to handle.

faqs.question: Why shouldn't two merle Aussies be bred together?
faqs.answer: Puppies who inherit two copies of the merle gene, called double merles, have a high risk of being deaf, blind, or both. Responsible breeders never breed merle to merle.

name: Yorkshire Terrier
coatColors: Blue and Tan, Black and Gold
exerciseNeeds: Short daily walks and indoor play
commonHealthIssues: Patellar luxation, portosystemic shunt, dental disease
dietNotes: Feed a small-breed diet in measured portions. Puppies need several small meals a day to prevent low blood sugar. Avoid overfeeding treats; a few extra calories matter a lot in a 5-pound dog. Dental chews sized for toy breeds can help with tartar.
trainingNotes: Yorkies are smart and can learn well, but they are independent. Keep sessions short and fun, with small food rewards. Be consistent with house training; a crate or puppy pen and frequent outings help. Train them like any other dog: sit, stay, come, and polite greetings. Socialize them early with people and dogs to prevent fearfulness or reactivity.
history:
The Yorkshire Terrier was developed in the mid-1800s in the industrial north of England, especially Yorkshire and Lancashire. Workers, many of whom had moved from Scotland to work in mills and mines, brought small terriers that were crossed to produce a dog that could catch rats in factories and mines. The Waterside Terrier, Clydesdale Terrier, and Paisley Terrier are among the breeds often named as ancestors.

A dog named Huddersfield Ben, born in 1865, became the breed's foundation sire through his show wins and many offspring. As the breed became smaller and silkier, it moved from mills to Victorian parlors as a fashionable companion. The AKC recognized the Yorkshire Terrier in 1885.
personalityDeepDive:
Yorkies are terriers first. They are bold, curious, and confident, often unaware of their size and willing to challenge much larger dogs. They are also affectionate and loyal to their people, and many like to be carried and cuddled.

They can be vocal and protective, sounding the alarm at every noise. Like many terriers, they may be bossy with other dogs and chase small animals.

With consistent training, Yorkies make lively, entertaining companions that enjoy games, walks, and learning tricks. Treating them like babies rather than dogs often leads to 'small dog syndrome': barking, guarding, and poor manners. They do best with owners who enjoy their spirit and give them structure.
livingWith:
Yorkies suit apartments and small homes well and need only modest exercise: short walks and indoor play. They are fragile, so they're best in homes with gentle older children rather than toddlers. Watch them around big dogs and on high furniture.

They are often vocal, so plan to train a quiet cue. Many dislike the cold and appreciate a sweater. House-training can take time, so consistency is important. Long coats need daily attention, while a short 'puppy cut' is easier for pets.
healthCareGuide:
Ask about patellar evaluations and eye exams on the parents. Common issues include luxating kneecaps, portosystemic liver shunt (signs include poor growth and odd behavior after meals; a bile acid test can screen for it), tracheal collapse (a honking cough, so use a harness instead of a collar), and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease of the hip.

Dental disease is very common because of their small, crowded mouths; daily brushing and regular cleanings help. Tiny puppies can develop low blood sugar if they miss meals.
funFact: Yorkies were originally bred to catch rats in textile mills.
famousQuote: A tiny terrier with a silky coat and a big-dog attitude: brave, bossy, devoted, and a lot more than a lap dog.
funFacts: Huddersfield Ben, born in 1865, is considered the father of the breed.
A Yorkie named Smoky served with US troops in World War II, helped run telegraph wire through a narrow pipe, and is often called one of the first therapy dogs.
Yorkie puppies are born black and tan and gradually develop their steel-blue and tan coats.
The Yorkie's coat is often compared to human hair because it keeps growing and has very little undercoat.
commonMisconceptions: That Yorkies are delicate lap dogs with no terrier instincts. They were bred to hunt rats and remain bold and spirited. Another misconception is that a 'teacup' Yorkie is a special variety; extra-tiny dogs are often bred for size at the expense of health.
idealOwnerProfile: Apartment dwellers, seniors, and adults or families with older children who want a small, lively, affectionate dog and are happy to keep up with grooming and dental care.
notGoodFor: Homes with toddlers, owners who want a quiet dog, people unwilling to keep up with grooming, and households with large, rough-playing dogs.
groomingGuide: A long show coat needs daily brushing and regular baths; most pet owners choose a short trim every six to eight weeks. Tie up or trim the hair above the eyes. Brush teeth daily if possible, trim nails regularly, and check ears.

faqs.question: Do Yorkies shed?
faqs.answer: Very little. Their hair-like coat has little undercoat, so shedding is minimal, which many allergy sufferers appreciate. The coat still needs regular brushing and trims.

faqs.question: Are Yorkies good with kids?
faqs.answer: They are better with older, gentle children. Their tiny size makes them easy to injure, and they may snap if handled roughly.

faqs.question: Do Yorkies bark a lot?
faqs.answer: They can. Yorkies are alert and vocal. Training a quiet cue and providing enough exercise and attention help.

faqs.question: How big do Yorkshire Terriers get?
faqs.answer: The breed standard calls for a weight of no more than 7 pounds. Most Yorkies are 4 to 7 pounds and about 7 to 8 inches tall.

faqs.question: Are Yorkies hard to house-train?
faqs.answer: They can be slower than some breeds. Consistent routines, frequent trips outside or to a potty area, and plenty of praise make a big difference.

faqs.question: Are teacup Yorkies healthy?
faqs.answer: 'Teacup' is not a recognized variety. Very small Yorkies are more prone to low blood sugar, fractures, and other health problems. Choose a breeder focused on health rather than tiny size.

name: Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
coatColors: Blenheim, Tri-color, Ruby, Black and Tan
commonHealthIssues: Mitral valve disease, syringomyelia, patellar luxation
dietNotes: Feed a quality small-breed diet in measured portions; Cavaliers love food and gain weight easily, which puts extra strain on the heart. Choose small training treats. Talk to your vet before choosing grain-free or boutique diets, given the breed's heart risks.
trainingNotes: Cavaliers are eager to please and respond well to gentle, reward-based training. They pick up house rules quickly and enjoy tricks, rally, and therapy-dog work. Build confidence with short periods alone from puppyhood to prevent separation anxiety. Practice recall in safe areas, since their chasing instinct can override it.
history:
Small spaniels were favorites of the British aristocracy for centuries, and King Charles II was so attached to his that the dogs took his name. Over time, breeders favored flatter faces and domed heads, creating the type now known in the US as the English Toy Spaniel.

In the 1920s, an American named Roswell Eldridge offered prize money at Crufts for spaniels resembling the old paintings, with longer noses and flat skulls. Breeders took up the challenge, and the Cavalier King Charles Spaniel was born from that effort. The Kennel Club recognized it as a separate breed in 1945, and the AKC recognized it in 1995.
personalityDeepDive:
Cavaliers are among the most gentle and affectionate breeds. They want to be with their people and usually like strangers, children, and other dogs just as much. They are adaptable: happy to snuggle on the couch or go for a hike.

They have some sporting spaniel instincts and may chase birds or squirrels, so a secure leash and fence matter. They are not watchdogs, and most bark only occasionally.

Their sensitivity is a strength and a weakness: they respond beautifully to gentle training but can become anxious if left alone for long periods. They are an ideal companion for people who are home a lot and want a sweet, sociable dog.
livingWith:
Cavaliers adapt well to apartments or houses, cities or countryside, as long as they get companionship and moderate exercise. Daily walks and play keep them fit. They do best when someone is home much of the day, since many struggle with separation.

They usually get along well with children, other dogs, and cats. Keep them leashed or in a fenced area because they may chase birds and squirrels.
healthCareGuide:
Health research is essential before buying a Cavalier. Mitral valve disease (MVD) affects most Cavaliers eventually, and often starts early. Ask breeders to show heart clearances from a cardiologist for both parents, and ideally follow MVD breeding protocols that use parents and grandparents with heart-clear results at specific ages.

Syringomyelia, a condition in which fluid-filled cavities form in the spinal cord, is also common; signs include scratching at the neck or shoulder without contact (phantom scratching), sensitivity to touch, and pain. MRI screening of breeding dogs helps. Ask about DNA tests for episodic falling and curly coat/dry eye syndrome, plus eye, hip, and knee evaluations.
funFact: King Charles II was so devoted to these spaniels that he decreed they must be allowed in any public place.
famousQuote: A gentle, affectionate toy spaniel that loves everyone, with heart health that every buyer must ask about.
funFacts: The breed is named after King Charles II, who was rarely seen without his spaniels.
The Blenheim color is named after Blenheim Palace, home of the Dukes of Marlborough, who kept red-and-white spaniels.
Cavaliers come in four colors: Blenheim, Tricolor, Ruby, and Black and Tan.
The breed was recreated in the 1920s after an American offered prize money for spaniels like those in old paintings.
commonMisconceptions: That a healthy-looking Cavalier puppy is enough. Heart disease and syringomyelia can develop later, so parental clearances matter. Another misconception is that Cavaliers and King Charles Spaniels are the same; in the US, the flatter-faced King Charles is a separate breed called the English Toy Spaniel.
idealOwnerProfile: Families, seniors, and singles who are home much of the day and want an affectionate, adaptable companion. Excellent for first-time owners who research heart health carefully.
notGoodFor: People away for long workdays, owners who want a guard dog, and anyone unable to cover potential cardiology costs or to choose a health-focused breeder.
groomingGuide: Brush the silky coat several times a week, especially the ears, chest, legs, and feet, where tangles form. Trim the hair between the paw pads. Clean the long ears weekly to prevent infections. Trim nails and brush teeth regularly.

faqs.question: Are Cavalier King Charles Spaniels healthy?
faqs.answer: They are prone to some serious inherited conditions, especially mitral valve disease and syringomyelia. Choose a breeder who screens hearts with a cardiologist and does MRI scans, and keep up with regular vet checkups.

faqs.question: Are Cavaliers good with children?
faqs.answer: Yes. Cavaliers are gentle, patient, and affectionate, making them excellent with respectful children.

faqs.question: Do Cavaliers shed?
faqs.answer: Yes, moderately. Their silky coat sheds year-round and needs brushing several times a week.

faqs.question: Can Cavaliers be left alone?
faqs.answer: Many struggle with being alone for long periods. Train short absences from puppyhood and avoid leaving them alone for full workdays.

faqs.question: How much exercise does a Cavalier need?
faqs.answer: About 30 to 45 minutes a day of walks and play. They are adaptable and happy to do more with active owners.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a Cavalier and a King Charles Spaniel?
faqs.answer: They are separate breeds. The King Charles Spaniel, called the English Toy Spaniel in the US, is smaller with a flat face and domed head. The Cavalier is larger with a longer nose and flat skull.

name: Doberman Pinscher
coatColors: Black and Rust, Red and Rust, Blue and Rust
commonHealthIssues: Dilated cardiomyopathy, Von Willebrand's disease, wobbler syndrome
dietNotes: Feed a quality large-breed diet in measured meals, typically twice a day to reduce bloat risk. Keep them lean and athletic. Talk to your vet about diet choices given the breed's heart risk, and avoid unproven boutique diets.
trainingNotes: Dobermans are among the easiest breeds to train for owners who are consistent. Use reward-based methods and clear rules. Socialize thoroughly from puppyhood so that protectiveness stays balanced. Obedience, tracking, nosework, agility, and protection sports with reputable clubs give them a job.
history:
The Doberman Pinscher was created around 1890 in Apolda, in the German state of Thuringia, by Karl Friedrich Louis Dobermann, a tax collector who also ran the local dog pound. He wanted a medium-large, intelligent, protective dog to accompany him on his rounds. The exact breeds used are not documented, but the old German Pinscher, Rottweiler, Weimaraner, black and tan terriers, and herding dogs are often suggested.

The breed spread quickly as a police and guard dog. The AKC recognized it in 1908. During World War II, Dobermans served with the US Marine Corps; a memorial to Marine war dogs on Guam features a Doberman.
personalityDeepDive:
Dobermans are smart, alert, and devoted. Many are 'velcro dogs' who want to be touching their people. With their family they are affectionate and playful; with strangers they tend to be watchful until introduced.

They have strong protective instincts and high energy, which need channeling through training and exercise. Dobermans are sensitive and respond best to fair, consistent handling. They are quick learners and can excel at obedience, tracking, protection sports, and agility.

A well-bred, well-raised Doberman is confident and stable, not aggressive. They thrive in homes where they are part of daily life rather than kept outside.
livingWith:
Dobermans need daily vigorous exercise and mental work. They are indoor dogs with a short coat and little body fat, so they get cold easily. They form strong bonds and may struggle with long periods alone.

They can be wonderful with children and other pets when raised together and trained, though their size and enthusiasm mean supervision with small children. Their alertness makes them effective watchdogs.
healthCareGuide:
Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the most serious health concern in Dobermans. Ask breeders about annual cardiac screening of the parents with a 24-hour Holter monitor and echocardiogram, and screen your own dog regularly starting in young adulthood. Early detection can allow treatment before symptoms appear.

Ask for a DNA test for von Willebrand disease (a bleeding disorder), plus OFA hip and thyroid results. Wobbler syndrome (a neck condition causing wobbly gait), bloat, and color dilution alopecia in blue and fawn dogs are also seen in the breed.
funFact: Dobermans were developed by a tax collector named Louis Dobermann who wanted a loyal guard dog.
famousQuote: Sleek, smart, and fiercely loyal: a protective companion that is affectionate at home and needs daily work.
funFacts: The breed is named after Louis Dobermann, a German tax collector who created it around 1890.
A bronze Doberman named Kurt is part of the US Marine Corps war dog memorial on Guam.
Outside North America the breed is usually called simply the Dobermann; the American name kept 'Pinscher'.
Dobermans come in black, red, blue, and fawn, each with rust markings.
commonMisconceptions: That Dobermans are vicious by nature. Modern, well-bred Dobermans are affectionate and stable. Another misconception is that ear cropping and tail docking are required; the AKC allows natural ears, and many owners now leave them uncropped.
idealOwnerProfile: Active, consistent owners who want a loyal, intelligent companion and protector and will invest time in training, exercise, and regular cardiac screening.
notGoodFor: Owners away for long hours, people who want a dog that can live outdoors, sedentary households, and anyone unwilling to commit to training.
groomingGuide: The short coat needs only a weekly brush with a rubber curry or grooming mitt. Trim nails regularly, clean ears (especially natural, uncropped ones), and brush teeth several times a week. Provide a coat in cold weather.

faqs.question: Are Dobermans aggressive?
faqs.answer: Not when well bred and well socialized. They are protective and watchful with strangers but typically affectionate and gentle with their families.

faqs.question: Are Dobermans good family dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, for active families who train them. They are loyal and affectionate and often good with children, though their size and energy need supervision with young kids.

faqs.question: How much exercise does a Doberman need?
faqs.answer: About 90 minutes a day of vigorous activity plus mental work such as training or scent games.

faqs.question: What heart problems do Dobermans have?
faqs.answer: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is common. Annual screening with a Holter monitor and echocardiogram helps detect it early, when treatment can help.

faqs.question: Do Dobermans shed?
faqs.answer: Lightly. Their short coat sheds a bit year-round and is easy to maintain with weekly brushing.

faqs.question: Do Dobermans need their ears cropped?
faqs.answer: No. Cropping is a cosmetic choice. Many Dobermans now keep their natural floppy ears, which the AKC standard allows.

As a member of the Non-Sporting Group, a diverse category of breeds that don't fit neatly into the other working classifications, the Kishu Ken carries hallmark traits of the group, visible in everything from how they move to how they read situations.
